revised_claim: Standard LSTK/EPC contracts in Southeast Asia and globally typically specify delay liquidated damages (LD) of 0.5% of contract price per week of delay, with a cap that varies by jurisdiction and sector: private-sector industrial EPC contracts commonly use 10–15% caps (industry practice across IFC/World Bank project finance contexts and published EPC templates), while Indonesian government procurement contracts (Perpres 16/2018, PUPR SSUK) apply a statutory rate of 1/1000 (0.1%) per calendar day — equivalent to ~0.7%/week — capped at the value of the performance guarantee (typically 5%). FIDIC Silver Book Sub-Clause 8.8 (1999) / Sub-Clause 8.7 (2017) intentionally leaves the rate blank for parties to fill in the Particular Conditions; it does not prescribe 0.5%/week. Malaysian standard forms (CIDB, JKR/PWD 203A, IEM) similarly leave the rate to the Appendix. The 0.5%/week rate is therefore a private-sector market convention — not a FIDIC or statutory standard — and is broadly consistent with market practice across power, process, and industrial EPC contracts. The 10–15% cap range is supported by published EPC templates (CT Green Bank/SunPower EPC template: 15% cap) and industry commentary (ACC article: 'most projects include a 10% to 15% cap'). The cost calculations in PP3.1 and PP3.2 using 0.5%/week are within the plausible range of market practice for private industrial EPC contracts in Malaysia/Indonesia, but should be disclosed as 'typical private EPC market convention' rather than a FIDIC or regulatory standard.

primary_sources.key_data: FIDIC official Q&A confirms Sub-Clause 8.7 (1999 Red/Yellow Books) and Particular Conditions (Silver Book) require the rate to be stated in the Appendix/Particular Conditions 'as a rate per day of delay' with a stated maximum — FIDIC does not prescribe a specific percentage. The rate is left blank.
primary_sources.note: This is the most authoritative FIDIC source available publicly. The full Silver Book text with Sub-Clause 8.8 requires purchase from FIDIC.

primary_sources.key_data: Cubic Electronics Sdn Bhd v Mars Telecommunications Sdn Bhd [2018] MLJU 1935 — Malaysian Federal Court confirmed LD clauses are enforceable under Contracts Act 1950 s.75 regardless of actual loss, provided the stipulated sum is not unreasonable. Burden now on contractor to prove unreasonableness. This confirms enforceability of market-standard LD clauses in Malaysia but does not specify a rate.

CIDB Standard Form of Contract for Building Works 2000, Clause 26.2(a): 'the Employer shall be entitled to recover from the Contractor Liquidated Damages calculated at the rate stated in the Appendix.' No prescribed rate — confirming that Malaysian standard forms leave the rate to negotiation, not a statutory 0.5%/week.

Indonesian government contracts under Perpres 16/2018 and PUPR SSUK use a statutory denda keterlambatan rate of 1/1000 (0.1%) of the contract value per calendar day, capped at the performance guarantee value. This is approximately 0.7%/week — higher than the 0.5%/week claimed — but applies to government (public) procurement only, not private industrial EPC contracts.

Confirms 10%–15% cap range as typical in EPC contracts: 'most projects include a 10% to 15% cap on performance liquidated damages' and 'contractors typically attempt to cap liquidated damages risk at a certain percentage of the contract price, which may range from 5% to 25%.'
Cites 0.5% per week with 5% cap as one FIDIC-inspired standard clause example. Also cites variant: 0.5% per week capped at 10% of delayed order value for equipment supply.

gap_confirmed: No primary source explicitly prescribes '0.5% per week' as a standard rate for industrial boiler EPC in SEA. FIDIC, CIDB, IEM, and JKR/PWD all leave the rate to the Appendix/Particular Conditions. The 0.5%/week figure is a widely-used private market convention documented in industry commentary and appears in representative EPC templates, but it is not codified in a statutory or FIDIC-mandated table.
recommended_disclosure: Cost calculations in PP3.1 and PP3.2 should be disclosed as follows: 'LD rate of 0.5% of contract price per week is used as a representative private-sector industrial EPC market convention (consistent with FIDIC Sub-Clause 8.7/8.8 framework under which parties typically negotiate 0.3%–1% per week). Cap of 10–15% is consistent with project-finance EPC market practice. For Indonesian government-procured projects, the statutory rate is higher (0.7%/week) with a lower cap (~5%). Actual contractual rates vary and should be confirmed against the specific contract.'
notes: 15 searches performed, 8 fetch attempts (4 successful, 4 failed due to PDF encoding or 403). FIDIC Silver Book full text requires purchase — the official FIDIC Q&A page confirms the framework but no prescribed rate. Indonesia statutory rate (Perpres 16/2018) contradicts the claimed rate direction: government-sector LD is actually higher (~0.7%/week), not lower, but with a lower cap (~5%). The 0.5%/week + 10–15% cap convention is best supported for private-sector industrial EPC in Malaysia/SEA by multiple industry legal commentaries and published contract templates. Primary gap: no Southeast Asia-specific court decision or arbitral award was found that explicitly validates 0.5%/week for industrial boiler/biomass EPC contracts. The Cubic Electronics 2018 Malaysian Federal Court decision provides strong enforceability context for LAD clauses in Malaysia under Contracts Act s.75 but does not specify a rate.
